references.text: The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus uses the same image of the camel and the needle's eye: 'It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God' ([ref:Matt 19:24|Matthew 19:24]).
The parallel passage in Mark with the same statement about the camel and the needle's eye, emphasizing how difficult it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God ([ref:Mark 10:25|Mark 10:25]).

The preceding verse where Jesus sees that the rich ruler has become sorrowful and says, 'How hard it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!' – which provides the immediate context for the needle's eye image ([ref:Luk 18:24|Luke 18:24]).

Jesus' answer to the disciples' despair: 'What is impossible for people is possible with God.' This shows that although it is impossible for the rich to save themselves, God can make it possible ([ref:Luk 18:27|Luke 18:27]).

In the Sermon on the Plain according to Luke, Jesus pronounces a 'woe' upon the rich: 'Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your comfort.' Wealth is an obstacle to entering the kingdom of God ([ref:Luk 6:24|Luke 6:24]).

Paul warns that those who want to be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and that love of money is a root of all kinds of evil – which expands on the dangers of wealth that Jesus speaks about ([ref:1 Tim 6:9-10|1 Timothy 6:9-10]).

The parable of the rich farmer who stores up treasures for himself but is not rich toward God. It illustrates why wealth can prevent someone from entering the kingdom of God ([ref:Luk 12:16-21|Luke 12:16-21]).

Jesus says that no servant can serve two masters – one cannot serve both God and Mammon. The power of wealth over the heart makes it difficult to enter the kingdom of God ([ref:Luk 16:13|Luke 16:13]).

Jeremiah's rhetorical question about whether a leopard can change its spots illustrates that for people it is impossible to change their nature – a parallel to the impossible image of the camel going through the needle's eye ([ref:Jer 13:23|Jeremiah 13:23]).

James urges the rich to boast in their humiliation, for they will pass away like the flower of the field. The fleeting nature of wealth and its danger to the soul sheds light on Jesus' words ([ref:Jak 1:10-11|James 1:10-11]).
